# Sum of Complex Integrals on Adjacent Intervals

## Theorem
Let $[a, b]$ be a closed real interval. Let $f: [a, b] \to \mathbb{C}$ be a continuous complex function. Let $c \in [a, b]$. Then:
$$ \int_a^c f(t) \,dt + \int_c^b f(t) \,dt = \int_a^b f(t) \,dt $$

## Proof
Let $u, v: [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be the real and imaginary parts of $f$, respectively. Thus, $f(t) = u(t) + i v(t)$ for all $t \in [a, b]$.
Since $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$, it follows that both $u$ and $v$ are continuous real-valued functions on $[a, b]$.
By the definition of the integral of a complex function, we have:
$$ \int_{\alpha}^{\beta} f(t) \,dt = \int_{\alpha}^{\beta} u(t) \,dt + i \int_{\alpha}^{\beta} v(t) \,dt $$
for any interval $[\alpha, \beta] \subseteq [a, b]$.
Therefore, we can write the sum of the two integrals as:
$$ \int_a^c f(t) \,dt + \int_c^b f(t) \,dt = \left( \int_a^c u(t) \,dt + i \int_a^c v(t) \,dt \right) + \left( \int_c^b u(t) \,dt + i \int_c^b v(t) \,dt \right) $$
By rearranging the terms, we group the real and imaginary parts:
$$ = \left( \int_a^c u(t) \,dt + \int_c^b u(t) \,dt \right) + i \left( \int_a^c v(t) \,dt + \int_c^b v(t) \,dt \right) $$
For real-valued continuous (and thus integrable) functions, the integral over adjacent intervals is additive. Thus:
$$ \int_a^c u(t) \,dt + \int_c^b u(t) \,dt = \int_a^b u(t) \,dt $$
and
$$ \int_a^c v(t) \,dt + \int_c^b v(t) \,dt = \int_a^b v(t) \,dt $$
Substituting these results back into the equation yields:
$$ \left( \int_a^b u(t) \,dt \right) + i \left( \int_a^b v(t) \,dt \right) $$
Which, by definition, is equal to:
$$ \int_a^b f(t) \,dt $$
Hence, the claim is proven.
